implementation_notes: The classic structure collapses into the guard: std::lock_guard locks the mutex in its constructor and unlocks it in its destructor, so the lock is a property of the lexical scope and every exit path - return, break, exception - releases it. In the small case the standard library is the layer supertype, so nothing has to be hand-written; std::unique_lock is the movable variant for locks that must be released early, moved or handed to a condition variable. The explicit lock()/unlock() pair is justified only where the mutex lifetime cannot be tied to a scope, such as dynamic locking inside allocators or a condition_variable wait loop.
pitfalls: A guard that is not bound to a name is destroyed immediately: std::lock_guard<std::mutex>(mu); and the brace form both construct a temporary, so the lock silently does not cover the following statements.
Recursive locking of a non-recursive std::mutex is undefined behaviour, and condition_variable::wait requires std::unique_lock rather than std::lock_guard.
A guard holds the lock for its whole scope, so I/O or callbacks inside the guarded scope become contention; scope the guard as narrowly as the invariant allows.

variants.name: C++17 std::scoped_lock and shared_mutex reader/writer guards
variants.implementation_notes: With C++17 the RAII contract gains two capabilities that change how much discipline the pattern needs: std::scoped_lock takes any number of mutexes and locks them with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm, so multi-object operations no longer depend on a hand-maintained global lock order, and std::shared_mutex with std::shared_lock expresses read/write locking so the framework can hand out shared locks to readers. The mechanism is still scope-bound release, so the choice against the C++11 variant is a capability-floor decision: use this variant when the toolchain is C++17 and operations either span several objects or are read-dominated.
pitfalls: std::shared_mutex serializes writers and can starve them under constant read load; measure before replacing a plain mutex, and note that upgrading a shared_lock is not possible - release and retake.

A shared_lock in a const member function requires the mutex to be mutable, and one shared_mutex across several objects does not fix lock-order coupling between separate mutexes; scoped_lock only orders the mutexes of a single call.
